description: We combine coding, design, and marketing to build a cool project and bring our ideas to life.
summary:
ReField helps a farmer who is bringing a field back into use after years of idleness decide what to sow in the first three seasons. In Ukraine about 2.2 million ha of cropland stood abandoned by 2024, and 472 thousand ha came back into cultivation that year (NASA Harvest). A field that sat idle returns to a different climate and a different weed and soil situation, and the farmer usually has little to go on.
 
ReField reads the field's history for 2016-2025 from NASA HLS 30 m imagery, shows how the district climate changed since the field was abandoned (NASA POWER), and adds fires (FIRMS), slope (NASADEM) and soil (SoilGrids). Based on the farmer's priority - water, income or soil - it suggests 2-3 alternative re-entry plans, and every step links to its source.
 
Where the data is too thin, ReField says "Not enough data - check in the field" and gives an inspection checklist instead of guessing. Every number carries a badge that says whether it is measured, modeled or reanalysis, and the Validation page shows how far the classifier can be trusted.
details:
What it does

ReField is a free web tool for one decision: a farmer is taking back a field that stood idle for several years and needs to choose what to sow first. Open the site, confirm the field has official clearance status, pick a field on the map, and ReField shows:

1. Field history. Each year from 2016 to 2025 gets a class - cultivated, fallow-or-abandoned or unknown - with a confidence from 0 to 1 and the number of clear observations behind it.

2. Climate gap. The growing season (April-October) in the 3 years before abandonment compared with the last 3 years: growing degree days, rainfall and days above 32 C. It is labeled as district background (~50 km), not the field itself.

3. Context. Fires near the field, slope, soil texture, organic carbon and pH. Each value has a badge: measured, model or reanalysis, plus its resolution.

4. Farmer priorities. A Water / Income / Soil switch reorders the crop options.

5. A 3-season re-entry plan. At least two alternatives side by side. Season 1 depends on rainfall: low rainfall leads to black fallow and saving moisture, enough rainfall leads to a cover crop or legumes. Each plan has a soil health line (seasons with legumes or cover vs seasons of bare soil), and every step links to its source.

6. An honest "unknown". Too few clear images or contradicting signs give "Not enough data - check in the field" and a short inspection checklist.

7. A safety gate. Analysis opens only after the user confirms the field has official clearance status. ReField does not assess mine or UXO safety, and coordinates are never stored.

How it works

The three demo fields are precomputed by a Python pipeline from NASA HLS v2 30 m imagery (Landsat and Sentinel-2) with Fmask cloud masking and 16-day medians, then classified year by year from NDVI phenology: a harvest drop means cultivated, a field that stays green in May and October without a harvest drop means idle grassland, a bare spring with a summer peak means a late crop. Fires, slope, soil, land cover and POWER climate are added and saved as JSON that the static site loads. For any other point on the map the site queries NASA POWER and ORNL MODIS live in the browser; fires, slope, soil and the climate gap are available for the demo fields only, and the site says so.

How far it can be trusted

We labeled 45 points in western and central Ukraine year by year from Sentinel-2 images (AI-assisted visual labels) and split them at random into a tuning half and a test half. On the held-out test half (15 points, 119 point-years) ReField agrees with the labels in 89% of the point-years where it gives an answer (74 of 83), 62% overall, and says "unknown" in 30%. Most losses are "unknown" from clouds or missing images, not wrong answers. A grid search over 7,776 threshold combinations on the tuning half found no setting that cut "unknown" without adding errors, so the thresholds stay as they are. A second blind AI pass over 25 random test point-years agreed with the original labels in 23 of 24 (1 unclear) - this checks label consistency, not ground truth.

Why we validate at all: a ready-made 10 m land cover map labeled two of our first three candidate fields as idle grassland, while the HLS series and Sentinel-2 images showed spring tillage, crop rows and harvest.

Benefits and intended impact

The farmer gets a field-specific starting plan instead of sowing by habit, and sees exactly which number is measured, modeled or missing. The same view helps agronomists, hromadas and recovery programs decide which returning fields need a closer look. The goal is fewer failed first seasons on returned land and crop choices that fit the climate the field returns to.

What makes it different

Field-history tools usually serve banks and buyers. ReField is built for the farmer at the moment of return: it combines how long the field stood idle with how the climate changed during those years, and it treats "I don't know" as a feature. Every number on screen says what it measures and at what resolution.

What we considered

- Safety: no claims about mines or UXO, only a pointer to official clearance.

- Honesty about scale: POWER describes the district (~50 km), the field is described at 30 m by HLS and NASADEM.

- Privacy: coordinates are not stored.

- Access: a light static site that works on a phone.

- Copyright: only open data and our own code, text and logo.

Limitations

ReField does not assess mine and UXO safety, soil contamination or land ownership. SoilGrids is a model estimate. Mowed grassland can look like a harvest in NDVI. The validation sample is small and the labels are AI-assisted visual labels, not field data. The full analysis exists for three demo fields; any other point gets a lighter live version.

Future work

1. Interviews with farmers, agronomists and hromadas, then a pilot on 3-5 fields returning in the 2026 season. Metric: hectares returned with a plan.

2. 100+ points labeled by two independent experts with some field checks; separate classes for fallow and abandoned land; recalibrated thresholds.

3. Full analysis for any field: server-side HLS, FIRMS, NASADEM and SoilGrids, a drawn field polygon, and the climate gap for any point (already ported to the browser and matched to the Python pipeline on all 35 seasons).

4. Regional crop parameters instead of global FAO EcoCrop ranges, and plan rules reviewed by an agronomist.

Tools

- Languages: Python 3.12, JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, CSS3; data in JSON, GeoJSON and CSV.

- Data pipeline: pystac-client, planetary-computer, earthaccess, odc-stac, xarray, rasterio, numpy, pandas, shapely, pyproj.

- Website: vanilla JavaScript and Leaflet with NASA GIBS layers, hosted as a static site on Vercel; code in a private GitHub repository.

- Hardware: a regular laptop. The site runs in any modern browser, including phones.

- Software: VS Code, Claude Code, Copernicus Browser.
